Senses.Explanation: To carry the cangue and submit one’s own indictment is to incriminate oneself by the very answer or claim offered in defense. Chan speakers use the legal image when someone’s words supply both the restraint and the charge against him. Muzhou Daoming applies it after a questioner claims that Muzhou knows; another Muzhou record uses it when a questioner asks where his speech went wrong. Cuiyan Kezhen gives it as the answer defining a person of the Way. The official Zheng Gongbu turns it back on Fenyang during their exchange.

DraftEvidence.ZenBend: A criminal procedure becomes an encounter verdict: the speaker does not need to be convicted from outside because his own words deliver the case.
DraftEvidence.CounterexampleOrLimit: The phrase marks self-incrimination in these exchanges; it does not describe an actual court sentence or every use of a cangue.

DifferentThingTest.Reason: The paired legal acts form one image of self-incrimination; they are not alternate readings of the same word.

DraftEvidence.AliasRationale: Probes preserve self-incrimination, restraint, charge sheet, and self-delivery.

ModifierControls.Finding: 擔枷 places the restraint on the speaker while 過狀 makes his own statement the submitted charge.

FamilyControls.Finding: The cangue alone lacks the self-submitted indictment.
